name: CQRS
intent: Use separate models for changing data (commands) and for reading it (queries), so each side can be shaped and scaled for its own job.
scenario: An online shop's orders have complicated business rules when written, but the website mostly shows simple lists such as 'my recent orders' and 'orders per customer', thousands of times more often than orders are placed.
problem: One data model has to serve two very different needs. A normalised model that is good for enforcing rules makes read queries slow and join-heavy. A denormalised model that is fast to read makes every write awkward and risks inconsistent copies. Under heavy read load, writes and reads also compete for the same database.

howItWorks.title: Commands change state, queries only read
howItWorks.text: A command (PlaceOrder) goes through the domain rules and changes state, and returns little or nothing. A query (GetRecentOrders) returns data and changes nothing. The two have separate code paths.

howItWorks.title: The write model enforces the rules
howItWorks.text: It stores data in the shape that makes validation and transactions easy: normalised, consistent, and small. It does not need to be pleasant to query.

howItWorks.title: Read models are built for the screens that use them
howItWorks.text: Each read model is a denormalised view shaped exactly like one query, such as an 'orders per customer' table. Reads become simple lookups with no joins, and can be served from a separate database or cache, scaled independently.

howItWorks.title: Events or change feeds keep them in sync
howItWorks.text: When the write side changes, it publishes an event (or a change record). A projector updates the read models. Because this happens after the write, read models are eventually consistent: for a moment they can be slightly behind.

howItWorks.title: Use it where it earns its keep
howItWorks.text: CQRS does not require event sourcing, though they are often combined. It adds moving parts and eventual consistency, so it is worth it for read-heavy or complex domains, and overkill for plain CRUD.

pros: Each side can use the best storage and shape for its job
Reads scale independently of writes, often with simple, fast queries
New read models can be added without touching the write side
Domain rules stay clean because they are not mixed with display needs
cons: More components, and more code than a single model
Read models are eventually consistent, so users can see stale data
Keeping projections correct and rebuildable takes care
whenToUse: Different screens need very different shapes of the same data
Business rules on writes are complex and benefit from a focused model
You already publish events and can feed projections from them
whenNotToUse: A simple CRUD application where one model serves everyone well
Users must read their own writes immediately and you cannot work around the lag
A small team that cannot afford the extra operational surface
pitfalls: Applying CQRS to a whole system instead of the parts that need it
Surprising users with stale reads right after they act (show their change optimistically, or read from the write side for them)
Read models that cannot be rebuilt, so one bad projection is permanent
Putting business logic in the projector instead of the write model

roles.label: Write model
roles.description: Enforces rules and stores the truth.
